To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
missing data in treatment effect estimation can be a serious problem and can lead to poor treatment effect estimates, but that selective imputation can be used to mitigate this problem.

(1) missing data in the treatment variable is a new missingness type that causes bias when naively imputating all data and (2) selective imputation can be used to mitigate the bias caused by missing data in treatment.

(i) naively imputating missing data leads to poor treatment effect estimation, (ii) selective imputation can lead to better treatment effect estimation than naively imputated data, and (iii) selective imputation leads to better treatment effect estimates than not imputating at all.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the problem of treatment effect estimation in data with missingness, where we identify a new type of missingness mechanism that is prevalent in practice and propose an imputation scheme that outperforms other solutions.
the following questions: (1) What is the best approach to deal with missingness when estimating treatment effects? (2) Can selective imputation be applied to a variety of learners?
the question of when and how to impute data in the context of estimating treatment effects from observational data.

selective imputation is a powerful tool to improve treatment effect estimation in the presence of missing data.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of treatment introduces a new missingness structure that is not captured by previous work.
missingness mechanisms are not well understood in treatment effect estimation, and that the presence of a treatment variable can lead to new missingness mechanisms.
missing data is a complex problem and that the standard approach of imputing all variables does not always work.
